speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This will place the CRL higher, in terms of capacity and usage, compared to, for example, the North East Line (NEL).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The CRL will also significantly enhance our network resilience as commuters will have many more routing options with the CRL connecting to other lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: What this means is that nearly half of the 30-plus new stations will be interchange stations and that means that every other station will be an exchange station where commuters can switch to another line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This will significantly enhance the resilience of our network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Both options are underground and construction of the tunnels for this stretch of CRL will be carried out using bored tunnelling, instead of the cut-and-cover approach.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Cut-and-cover means you cut through like a huge bulldozer and chop down whatever is in between, then you build the tunnel and you cover it up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: With bored tunnelling, you avoid all the trauma and damages above the tunnel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: About 40 metres – or 12 storeys – below ground level.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: More importantly, at that level, this is what geologists call the hard bedrock level.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In our case, this is the Bukit Timah granite.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: At this level, there are no vegetation, no trees, no animals.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Under this option, there will not be any construction of infrastructure at surface level within the CCNR.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The skirting alignment option, on the other hand, is about nine kilometres long.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Because it is nine kilometres long, it will require longer tunnels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Member suggested that the skirting alignment could potentially serve more residents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: However, the catchment there is already served by the Circle Line and the upcoming Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Page: 15 The CRL is a massive project and the Government will decide on its entire alignment only after making a total assessment, including financial viability, technical feasibility and other relevant considerations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is only one of the many studies which we need to undertake to help us determine the best alignment for the stretch of the CRL in the vicinity of the CCNR.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Later, my colleague in the Ministry of National Development (MND) will provide some details on the EIA and also describe how the Government agencies are working closely with the nature groups on the EIA.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It has been a very productive collaboration, although much remains to be done.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As the alignments can have a different impact on the environment, commuters, taxpayers, businesses and home owners, the Government has a responsibility to study both options thoroughly.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Besides the EIA, there are upcoming technical site investigation works which will allow us to determine the soil profile and condition.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This will feed into the Engineering Feasibility study.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Only after all these environmental and technical studies on both possible alignments have been completed and taking into account the potential impact on the nature reserve, the travelling distance and time for commuters, the cost to taxpayers and the potential acquisition of homes and businesses, will we be able to make an informed decision on the project and its exact alignment.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: There will be many more public consultations so that we can adequately factor in all views.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, the EIA Phase 1 report is available online.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, could the Minister clarify what is the total cost for the construction of the CRL and what percentage increase that is of the total construction cost if we use the skirting alignment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, if we do use the skirting alignment, could the Minister clarify exactly which buildings or houses may need to be acquired?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As I have said, this is a massive project and, usually, it would take easily four to five years for all the important studies to be made.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In fact, although the EIA is published now, this is a product of two years of discussions and consultations.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In this particular instance, it is because of the interests of nature groups and the sensitivity of the possible impact of any work of this part of the CRL on the nature reserve that the issue now surfaces.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We have some idea because this is not the first time we are building an MRT line.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We can have some idea about how much the cost will be but one can never be sure because what happens underground is invisible; we do not know.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And soil conditions, even though we are a tiny little red dot, the geology of east and west, north and south, can be very different.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is why it is so important to do a thorough site investigation.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The EIA, after two years of study, is now published online.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: By the gazette requirements, Singaporeans, interest Page: 16 groups, stakeholders, are invited to give their comments.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Sorry for the long reply, but there are many questions which remain unanswered.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: What I urge of Singaporeans is this: keep an open mind.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Go with the facts, keep an open mind and look for the evidence.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It was a good movie because it was not just for the kids; it carries important values and some political messages.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It tells the story of a little female bunny whose ambition is to bring about justice and change the world, and she wants to be a police officer.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The police world at that time was largely monopolised by larger animal species and all males.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But she was determined to be a police officer.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, she had to fight stereotyping, sexism, racism, bias and prejudice.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In the end, she succeeded through wit and effort, and demonstrated what she can achieve.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Likewise, for the EIA, let us keep an open mind.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I have read some of the very toxic comments on the EIA.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: They were made even before the EIA was published.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think there is an English word for that and, that is, bias, prejudice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I just want to find out if maintenance cost will also be considered, besides the capital cost in the study.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As I have said, this four- to five-year study is a total impact study.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, I am not opting for one or the other yet.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But there have been comments about the second option that, of course, clearly, anybody reading the map would know that it will take a longer route, takes a longer time.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: And to the commuters, it means extra time.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The media have been guessing the figures; they say "an extra four minutes".

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Some people commented, "Well, that is just a few minutes." I am not so sure we can brush aside the extra six minutes just like that because, in the mindset of the MRT commuters, an extra half a minute is already terrible.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: When the train has a disruption, causing an extra one minute of delay, commuters can, within that one minute, send off, maybe, 100 tweets to flame LTA or SMRT.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, an extra one minute is a lot of time, let alone six minutes!

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That is why, in the rail industry, they define disruption as anything that causes delay of more than five minutes; and six is more than five.
